blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: DR OWEN ARTHURS (sworn)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Would you start by identifying yourself, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm Owen John Arthurs.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And your profession, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm a consultant paediatric radiologist at Great Ormond Street Hospital in London.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: A paediatric radiologist. What does a paediatric radiologist do, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: A radiologist is a specialist in images and image interpretation and my special interest is in doing that in children.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. And your qualifications, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm a fellow of the Royal College of Radiologists, I'm a fellow of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, and I hold a PhD in imaging, and I am now professor of radiology at Great Ormond Street Hospital.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. You have reviewed many of the children in this case, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I have.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The two that I'm going to ask you about today are [Baby A] and [Baby B]. And you have written several reports on each; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I have.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Just as a little bit of background, can we start with [Baby A] first. I think you were given information about [Baby A]'s birth, his weight at birth, his gestation at birth and also details of when he died?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And I won't ask you to repeat those because the jury has already heard that information. But what in general terms were you invited or instructed to do?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So I was to review the imaging of [Baby A]. He had several X-rays taken when he was alive. He also had several Xrays taken after he died, which were done in Alder Hey.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And Alder Hey is the children's hospital in Liverpool, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. From time to time some of the witnesses in this case use the phrase "radiograph"; is that the same as an Xray or is it different?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Technically, the X-ray is the beam that passes through the body to produce the image, so the image is technically a radiograph, but the popular term for the images has become "Xray images", so use of the term X-rays is fine.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we deal first, if we may, with material other than the images that you've seen. Were you sent reports from other medical practitioners?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I have, and I think I've detailed those in my reports.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. They included, I think, three reports from Dr Dewi Evans?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And a report from Dr Andreas Marnerides?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Dealing with the in-life X-rays first then if we may, if we could just put these on the screen to remind the jury. They are tiles 31, 128 -- I'm not going to go to these individually -- thank you. This is just for the jury's benefit if they want the information at the moment. 128 is the next tile. 142. And finally, 156.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can we just go to that image, please, the one at 156?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Dr Arthurs, is it right to say that, broadly speaking, those four images are similar?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And they're all slightly different because they're taken at different times of a child from not in exactly the same position. Is there anything unusual about any of the four images?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In [Baby A], no, there's nothing particularly remarkable about the images that we have in terms of his heart and lungs. I think the only comment that I made was about the umbilical catheter that was in slightly the wrong place.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. We've heard some of the treating doctors talk about that. So nothing remarkable about those images.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just so that the jury have this as a reference -- and this is the first time we've actually looked at any of the X-rays, really -- we can see at the bottom right-hand edge of the picture, there is a date and timestamp. Is that stamped by the machine?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It's either stamped by the machine or by the radiographer when they acquire the X-ray, so it's a date of acquisition to document exactly when it was done.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes, and in this context does acquisition mean taking the picture?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's right, apologies.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Top left-hand corner, name, sex, presumably an individualised identification number for the child concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Hospital number, so that will be Countess of Chester, and then a six, seven or eight-digit number.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Is there any significance in any of the other --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, they show the parameters that have been used by the machine to take the image.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Right. When you -- well, you were also shown or given seven images of [Baby A] that had been taken after his death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Those images were taken, as you've told us, as Alder Hey?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And taken on 11 June?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think they were taken on the 10th, actually.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I beg your pardon.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There's an error in some of the documentation, but yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I'd just like to show you one of those images, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Just to orientate -- well, could you orientate us, please, as to what we're seeing here?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do the jury have the image that I can see here --
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- in the quality that I can see it? Because I think the quality of what's been projected is not as good.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Can you all see it on the screens in front of you?
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: This is image taken laterally through the baby with the baby lying down. The head is on the left-hand side of the image and the pelvis -- you can see the two femurs on the right-hand side of the image as you are looking at it. The bones of the spine are shown all the way in sequence along the bottom. And in fact, just beneath the skull, you can see some of the tubes and those are the things that were still in place. So there's an endotracheal tube, for example, crossing the neck.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Is that at the top of the neck?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The top, yes. There are two lines and there's a nasogastric tube as well just below that.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So X-rays show bones as white because they prevent the X-rays from going through them and they show gas and air, for example, as black.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Just for the purposes of general education, really, because these issues become relevant at a later stage although they're not relevant to this particular case.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What can we see just to the left of where the femurs start, that sort of dark area there?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If you move your cursor up, this is gas within the bowel, a normal feature of post-mortem radiographs. The block of gas that is the black area which is to the left of that, further up in the body, is gas within the heart.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. Below the heart that we can see there, is that the nasogastric tube which is running --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right, that's the white tube that ends just there (indicating). So that would be presumably in the stomach.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. Is there anything that's unusual about this radiograph --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. The comment I made about this radiograph is that you can also see, as well as all the normal expected gas that you would see in a baby in a post-mortem state, you can also see a line of gas just in front of the spine.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So that runs almost from there (indicating) almost all the way up to there (indicating), that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Okay. Would you normally expect to see that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. That's an unusual finding.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So far as how it comes to be there, what are the possibilities from your perspective?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that finding is so unusual that I reviewed several of my existing cases in the series of radiographs that we have at Great Ormond Street to try and identify in what circumstances that might occur. In my report I've gone in length into the possible circumstances in which we often see that type of gas.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So firstly, it's quite unusual. So in several hundred radiographs of babies who have died of natural causes, we don't see gas in that location.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Right. Let's just take this slowly, if we may, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: A death from natural causes, you just don't see that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We don't see that. That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And so far as unnatural causes are concerned, what are the possibilities?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So if there's been a severe fracture somewhere in the body then gas could be introduced and then circulated and it could be seen there.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Right. Now, this is your day-to-day experience, we're all novices. How does a fracture introduce air into the body in a position like this?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't mean a fracture of a bone, a simple bone, something like that. Something like a road traffic accident, if you were to have a fracture through your skull base, it might also break the blood vessels and then air can track into the blood vessels. So what I'm talking about is severe road traffic accidents, those kind of things.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Okay. So we know this child was in hospital from birth to death, so we can exclude road traffic accidents?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: What's the next possibility?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The other circumstance in which we've seen it has been overwhelming infection, sepsis.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. Sepsis is a term that most jurors will have heard.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It may be that some of them, like me, don't really understand what it means. What is sepsis?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sepsis is essentially overwhelming infection in most of the organs of the body.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: If it was a case of sepsis, would you see evidence on the radiograph, on the X-ray, of problems with the organs as well?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So, no, not always because, as you can see, what we mainly see on X-rays are bones and gas, and we can't distinguish very much else of the other soft tissues.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Okay. So in order to determine whether or not sepsis was a possibility in this case, what would the jury have to look at in terms of other evidence in the case?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This baby died, so there would have been an autopsy, and there would be clear identifiers from a pathology point of view as to whether or not the baby had overwhelming infection.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Right. On the basis that we exclude that as a possibility, what's the next possibility?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We have seen it occasionally, and very occasionally, in babies who have died outside of hospital. So the term for
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: unexplained death outside of hospital in infancy is S-U-D-I, SUDI, or sudden unexplained death in infancy.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Why do you put the restriction on babies who die outside hospital rather than including those who die in hospital in this context?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: SUDI is effectively a diagnosis of exclusion when all other things have been excluded in an otherwise well baby who wasn't being treated for anything, who went home, was feeding normally, et cetera, et cetera, and then unexpectedly collapsed at home. It is a recognised phenomenon that occurs in babies in the age of about 3 to 9 months. Again, a pathologist would be able to tell you much more about SUDI as a concept than I will.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: But this case plainly, for the reasons you've given us, doesn't fall into that category?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So what is the next possibility, please, Dr Arthurs?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We have seen it in some children who have undergone extensive resuscitation. I am just referring to my report, where we didn't see this very commonly on radiographs in that circumstance, but we are now performing CT scans, which are more detailed scans, of babies who have had died, which allows us to see smaller locules of gas and smaller and smaller -- better imaging, effectively.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So a CT scan is more discriminating?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Okay. Sorry, I interrupted you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, no. In that sense we have seen it occasionally following resuscitation and the premise is that -- we hypothesise that there is some natural gas in the body after death and it is possible therefore the resuscitation could circulate it around if it were successful in moving blood around with gas in it.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Are there any other possibilities as to how this gas got there?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So if you end at that point, effectively this is unexplained.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We do know that the baby had an umbilical venous catheter in situ and we do know that gas can be introduced into vessels through catheters and devices that medical people have put there.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So through cannulas, through long lines, through umbilical catheters, you can introduce gas.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: We know as a matter of evidence that there was also a long line in this child.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: It had been removed by the time these images were taken.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. The umbilical venous catheter actually is still in.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes, but the long line had been removed?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Can gas -- is it possible that the gas was introduced via one or other of those lines?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it's possible.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Is the appearance of the gas that we see in the image on the screen consistent with that as a method of introduction?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. So the sensible, most pragmatic conclusion to bring would be that in the absence of any other explanation, that would be an alternative explanation.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: But lest we read too much into it in isolation, is what we see in the image diagnostic of, ie does it say, yes, that is definitely how this gas was introduced?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, it doesn't. All the image shows you is gas in one of the large vessels of the body on a post-mortem radiograph of a small baby.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Have you ever seen this much gas in a child's body that hasn't been explained?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Only in one other case, which I think we'll discuss later on.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: This is one of the other children in this case?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So far as your opinion was concerned relating to this radiological finding in the body of [Baby A], what was your final opinion, please, doctor?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So my opinion was that this was an unusual appearance.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: This is not typical of any of the radiographs we normally see in this circumstance, and in the absence of any other explanation, this appearance is consistent with but not diagnostic of air being administered.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: What some might call an air embolus?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I'm not sure I would say this is evidence of an air embolus, but I think this would be consistent with air having been administered.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. All right. Just so that the jury understand why my use of language is incorrect, could you explain why air embolus isn't the correct label to put on what you can see in the image?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: To me an air embolus is effectively a cause of death, so sufficient air having been entered into the body and which kills the patient. I am not sure you can say that that's what's happened from this image.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And you're looking at it from your --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Purely from a radiological perspective.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So you're not taking into account any of the other evidence at all in the case?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: You're looking at the image and saying what you can see with your expertise from that image?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we turn to the case of [Baby B], please, [Baby A]'s sister?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, Dr Arthurs, were you approached to consider the evidence in the case of [Baby B]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's right, I was.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And did you review a number of images in her case?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Were they dated -- I'm not going to run through them as I did with the other case. Were they dated the 8th and 10 June?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: 2015, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. And taken at various times on those dates.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Is there anything that you saw in any of the images of [Baby B] that were unusual?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. In my report I've gone through six radiographs.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: [Baby B] was 31 weeks, so premature. [Baby B] shows some changes in lungs, which are that of premature lung disease, which would be expected, and there are no real other abnormalities to comment upon from a radiological perspective.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Does the lack of abnormalities from a radiological perspective inform the issue of whether or not anyone injected air into [Baby B]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think we need to consider that separately to [Baby B]'s images.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So if we consider an air embolus as a concept, in my experience we very rarely see air embolus as a cause of death or as a radiological diagnosis.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Why is that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There are several reasons. One is that very, very small amounts of air probably enter the body quite often when we give injections or those sort of things. We never take images of those, they never cause any problems, they disappear on their own and they -- so clinically, the baby and the child is asymptomatic.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: An air embolus to the point where it causes clinical symptoms is usually so massive that the last thing someone is rushing to do is to do an X-ray. So they would be so busy trying to resuscitate the child at all costs that very rarely is there
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: an X-ray at the same time to demonstrate that that was what happened.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So in the context of the jury having the issue to decide as to whether or not there was an air embolus in [Baby B]'s case, does the image help either for or against that as a proposition?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. It doesn't help for or against. So the absence of air doesn't mean that that didn't happen and then the air has disappeared. The presence of air would help obviously make that -- but you can understand why that very rarely, rarely occurs.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Would you remain there, please, Dr Arthurs? It may be that there are some further questions for you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
I just have some general questions to ask you about air in the body and your analysis of that, Dr Arthurs.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And then I'll look at the two cases that we've looked at here, but there may not be a great deal extra that I need to ask you about them. Just to confirm some general points, radiographic evidence of air embolus is rare, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: What you're able to tell us is that where you do encounter air in the system, particularly I am talking about in images taken during life, that is caused by medical procedures or the placement of lines into the patient's body?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That's usually the scenario.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And indeed, on post-mortem imaging, that's another regular explanation for how it is that air could be present?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Could you rephrase that?
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Well, on post-mortem imaging, the presence of air may also be the result of medical procedures or placement?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's reasonable.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I'll leave the question of how often out of it for the time being.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: We may hear more about this later, but just so the jury can keep up with where we are in talking about this, Dr Arthurs, when we talk about air entering the body because of the placement of vascular lines, that refers to the potential for something like a UVC, that we've heard about, or a long line being open to the air for long enough for air to pass through that and into the patient's body?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And that's something that can happen in practice?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Would you agree that it is rare to identify air embolus from radiographic imaging?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you a few questions about air in the body in life and then about the post-mortem situation.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we want to be able to identify and accurately diagnose air embolism in images in life, you would require imaging that showed the presence of air in blood vessels where there is no other explanation for the air being there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Um... You...
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Apart from -- no other explanation apart from being introduced externally.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. I think that you would -- in order to... So in order to see air on images in life, you would seek an explanation as to how they got there, one of which could be that they had entered the body through medical administration. Is that the question you were asking?
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Well, what I'm asking really is this, that the gold standard of identifying air embolus would be, first of all, an image showing the presence of air in the body in life?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So that I disagree with. That isn't the gold standard.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: As we have said --
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: What is the gold standard, let me ask?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It would be a clinical diagnosis as the most likely cause or potentially it would be identifiable at post-mortem. I
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: think the assumption that an image is needed to prove that air embolus occurred is wrong for precisely the reasons that we've given.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Because you have to look at it in the context of the history and all clinical findings?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: That's what I was going to ask. So what you have to do is look at the imaging and then you or you and others will look at the imaging together with the surrounding circumstances?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So far as imaging post-mortem, so after death, is concerned, you've explained to us that doing the research or the studies you've done, you wouldn't normally expect to find gas in the vessel or the vessels that we see on the image we've looked at?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Right. Would you say that in general, the significance of gas in the large vessels on post-mortem radiographs is not known?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I would say that when we see it, we usually have an explanation for it in the examples that I have given already.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Post-mortem gas in the body is a natural phenomenon, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So you may well expect to find, in your work, gas in various parts of the body after death?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And the build-up of gas after death can commence quite quickly, can't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: (Overspeaking) to start?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't think anybody knows how quickly but, yes, it can and seeing gas on images in normal vessels on post-mortem radiographs is common, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Is it the case that the more time passes, the greater the quantity of air -- the greater the quantity of gas?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think that's logical but I'm not sure that's necessarily proven.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: When you give us the conclusion or the opinion that the gas in the vessels is an unusual finding, where you've said that, is that something that's based on your own research from your own cases in your clinical work?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, and it's based on published literature that that's not a common phenomenon, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: In your reports you set out in some detail why it is that you say that, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Can I just explore that with you so we understand what you mean by that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, of course.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The review of cases that you have undertaken took you to a conclusion that you might expect to find that gas in 25% or fewer cases; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: My Lord, perhaps I should explain the reason why I went and did that review of the cases that I set out in my report.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I'm going to -- with his Lordship's leave I am going to take you through that, but I leave it to you to answer it how you wish.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: So when first we saw the gas in those locations, for me to be able to say that it is unusual, I had to go back and review cases because we know that gas is common in the heart, in some of the other locations, so I posed it to myself: perhaps we actually do see this commonly and we haven't appreciated it previously. So the reason to go back and investigate all of the children that we have is to see whether I could actually make the statement "this is unusual" with any degree of confidence. And there are three studies that I went through, one of which is published, based on CT, of children who have died and then more extensively going back through several babies who have died in our unit in a teaching case that we have and the conclusion from that is that it is indeed unusual.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And you give a figure in your report -- I'm looking at page 499, so this is the report dated 19 May 2020, it's page 8 of that report -- at page 10 of that report.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. So the figures I came up with in looking back through different groups was that approximately a quarter of the babies that we looked at had gas in the large vessels.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Right. So when you say you give us the figure that -it's an unusual finding to find gas there in terms of your research, that translates to 25% of the cases which you have gone through, that's what you found?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Right. I'm not going to question you about whether 25% is unusual or not, but that's the way you characterise 25%?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: 25% of the children that we came across, the majority of whom had an explanation.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: As to how you get to that, I just want to ask this.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You'll be familiar, Dr Arthurs, with evidence-based medicine, won't you, that approach?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: For those of us who aren't so familiar, that means basing an opinion on sound research; that's right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Recognising deficiencies in it and recognising where we simply don't know?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: When we come to look at the cases upon which you base your conclusion, there's a published paper you looked at, written by Barber and others, isn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's a paper on which I was a senior author, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: In that case, and I'm going to go through this so we can follow why we get to you saying unusual, in that case -- and you refer to this at page 10 of your report -- you found 60% of the children had gas in some location of their body after death.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So that's where you started on the report you worked on.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But when you looked at that, you saw that dealt with children whose average age was 2 years, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. These are older children and that study used CT.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So you then turned from that work to records at your own hospital, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: If we're going to have research and an evaluation of how often something comes before you in your work, the best research will be designed specifically to investigate an issue, won't it, it's prospective?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So it will define what it's looking into, won't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Are you arguing that we should have done a study --
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I just want to go through what you did do.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: It will control variables, things that can change?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: It will be conducted objectively, by which I mean, for example, the person reviewing the X-rays in that research may be masked from other clinical information?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: When you came to do your research, you had already -- I'm not being critical of you for this, it's inevitable, but you'd already been provided with an outline of what the investigation was about, hadn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: For the purposes of this I'd been provided with a hypothesis.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: A hypothesis, yes. If you're engaging in specific research you would try to have as wide a pool of subjects to base your research on as possible?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, which are representative of the question in hand.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And then the research would be what's called peer reviewed?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Which means that other specialists can look at it critically and assess it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: In coming to the finding that this is unusual, and the figure of 25%, what you did was to begin by narrowing down 500 cases that you had at Great Ormond Street, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Of those 500, a very large number of them were foetuses or stillborn, weren't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. That's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I just pause there to say, the hospital where you work is Great Ormond Street, isn't it, Dr Arthurs?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: You then narrowed down from those 500 to children who are under the age of 1 when they died; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Just pausing there, I'm going to carry on. Neonates are a specific group of babies, aren't they, as in 1 to 4 weeks as a rule?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And one cannot simply take studies of older babies or children as being indicative of what happens with a neonate in the period of 1 to 4 weeks?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, but that wasn't the purpose of what I was doing here.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: No, you were looking to see the occurrence of gas in those vessels?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. Of the 100 who were under the age of 1 when they died, you narrowed that down then to 38 children who were under 2 months of age at the time of death?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So we're now moving on from the 500 cases where I went through to look at their X-rays --
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- and I found six cases in slightly older children where gas was identifiable on the large vessels.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And of those, five had had traumatic injuries and the sixth child had died of sepsis. So in fact there was an explanation for the gas in the great vessels on all of those children from my radiographic study or the investigation that I did of their cases that I had.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: However, I then went into detail into the CT scans that we have on children under the age of 1, and I found 100 cases of those, of which 38 were babies under 2 months of age. So of those I found eight cases where they had gas in the great vessels and they had died of trauma, road traffic accidents, sudden unexpected death in infancy, congenital heart disease, and disseminated malignancy. So we had found no unexplained cases of gas in that location after a detailed review.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Your findings though are based, let's get this clear, on the basis of eight out of 38 babies; yes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So my findings are based on the case review that we have, which is probably the largest available.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The review you did comes down to narrowing it down to 38 babies who were under 2 months, that's where you get to?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: It can't be said from the information you have that that's representative of babies who are 1, 2 or 3 days old?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it's representative of the typical deaths that we encounter that are referred to Great Ormond Street Hospital.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Which itself is a particular class of work, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: It's not necessarily representative of every neonatal unit in the country, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's representative of perinatal autopsy in the types of babies who need a cause of death established.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: But the figures you're giving us, to be clear, are not based upon neonates in the first few days of life who are preterm exclusively, are they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The vast majority of those don't die.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: But the figures we have -- did your study group focus upon neonates 1 to 3 days old or a week old who were preterm?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can't tell you exactly from there, but they will have been included in the study if they died at my hospital.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: You can't tell us though?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: You can't tell us how much time, can you, passed from death to imaging in the cases that you're relying upon, can you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And you can't tell us, for instance, things like the specific temperatures in which, sadly, the bodies were kept before imaging was taken?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The 4 degrees is the standard temperature that they're kept in the mortuary refrigerator.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And the particular circumstances of death that we are dealing with in this case are not replicated, I'm talking the clinical circumstances, are not replicated in your work, are they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: How do you mean they're not replicated?
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: You were unable to identify from the children you looked at, Dr Arthurs, any that died in circumstances clinically that are the same or similar to the ones we're dealing with in this case, the circumstances of death?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. In the sense that the circumstances of death of these children are quite unusual, it would be reasonable that none of them were represented in the sample that I looked at.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The point I'm making, I hope clearly and respectfully, is there are many variables that can apply to a study when research is conducted upon it, aren't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And what you rely upon in telling us that you wouldn't normally expect to find gas in the vessels post-mortem is in effect, and I don't say this disrespectfully, but an informal review of cases from your own institution, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it's what you would call an observational study or clinical experience.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: But it's not a controlled study, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm trying to imagine how you would do a controlled study.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Well, I'm not asking you to imagine how. The proper approach would be to have a controlled study, if at all possible, wouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And what would a controlled study look like? What are the variables that we're trying to control in this particular circumstance?
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I'm not the claiming to be the expert, Dr Arthurs, I am asking you to confirm that this isn't a study with any set controls on it. It's made out of what you could find out of records looking through what you had at Great Ormond Street, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's what an observational study is.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Again not disrespectfully, but it lacks objectivity and independence in that it is conducted by you looking into a theory that you've been asked to consider?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it lacks objectivity in the sense that it's an observational study of what data was available at the time. I'm trying to understand -- I think your question is directed at this, that an alternative study could have been done and that is why this study is insufficient?
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: No, I'm looking at ways in which this may come below a higher standard of evidence-based medical research.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Oh, I see.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: That's why I began by asking that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So observational studies and clinical experience are not the highest levels of evidence-based medicine. However, sometimes they are the only evidence that we have on which some conclusions can be drawn.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And do you agree that --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just let him finish. Are you finished?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's what I have tried to provide to the court to try and contextualise how commonly this occurs, some potential explanations for it, and with the deficiencies, as you have kindly pointed out, in doing so, that is the basis on which I can provide my evidence here today.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So it's quite clear, and it's not meant to be discourteous or difficult in any way, but if we are expected to rely upon what you tell us, I'm anxious that we explain to the jury the circumstances in which you come to that assessment.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it's entirely reasonable.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. The study that you conducted, based on material from your own institution, has not -- again this isn't to be rude -been peer-reviewed or validated by anyone beyond what you're telling us now?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And it may well be that you have no alternative but to work with the numbers of babies you work with, but we come down to what you find in the case of eight babies out 38, don't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is my clinical experience.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. I'm not being critical of that and I'm not saying it's easy to do, but when we hear the finding that it is not what you'd normally expect or it's unusual, that is what that finding is based upon?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And I think the figure which that works out at, as a simple bit of maths, is in 25% of those cases there was gas in the great vessels post-mortem?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right, the majority of which had an explanation.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. Moving on to other ways in which we might find air in the system. We've dealt with air entering the system because of medical procedures or the medical profession.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You accept, do you, Dr Arthurs, that air may enter the system as a result of CPR, the resuscitation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't think air enters the system as a result of --
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Is liberated within the system as a result --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: -- but can be distributed.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: It can be distributed. And so if there has been resuscitation that has taken place, independently of the 25% point, that may be what's called a differential diagnosis? That's an alternative explanation for the air that we find.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it's an alternative explanation, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Where [Baby A] is concerned, there are a number of potential explanations for the air that we see in the X-ray that we looked at, is that right, Dr Arthurs?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There are a number of potential explanations, that's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And subject to all the circumstances, they can be assessed, but the potential explanations that you provide us with is air being introduced from outside, what was called at one point air embolus, if I recall.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: You make the point, well, air embolus presupposes that someone's -- the way you put it, it presupposes a cause of death, how it was done.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: From the radiographs, you can't say that; that's right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: But you can say one possibility is air coming in from outside?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Another possibility is post-mortem changes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Which is what we're looking at with the 25% figure and the research.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: (Witness nods).
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Another explanation is resuscitation, potentially?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: What you can say, concluding all of that, is that, therefore, air being present where it was found is consistent with an air embolus, but it isn't diagnostic of it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And it could be consistent with the other explanations we've looked at as well, depending upon the overall circumstances?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: In the case of [Baby B], what you identified, Dr Arthurs, from the chest radiographs you saw, suggests in addition to your conclusion you identified radiographs showing "mild lung disease of prematurity and its complications"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The radiograph -- one radiograph you saw is dated 10 June 2015, taken at 01.09?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The jury will know from evidence, and you may or may not know, that the collapse takes place round about 00.30.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: (Witness nods).
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So that means that radiograph is taken about 40 minutes after the time of collapse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And on that radiograph, there are no radiographic features to support air embolus, are there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that radiograph doesn't show a significant abnormality.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Arthurs.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Re-examination by MR JOHNSON
Just dealing with that last point, Dr Arthurs, the absence of a significant abnormality. What can we read into that either way, given the time frame that's just been explained to you?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can only speak to the radiographs, but I don't think you can conclude anything either way.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: No. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It may be that I misunderstood the questioning, but it appeared that one of the criticisms of your reviews of other cases was that in effect you were comparing apples with oranges, putting it in layman's terms.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Would it have been possible to do your exercise any other way than how you did it? In other words, look at other cases and try and contextualise them to the facts of this case?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think it's very difficult to come up with hypothetical ways in which something can have occurred. What I have tried to do is present what is quite a large body of evidence of how children and babies normally die and the circumstances and what we see on the imaging. So by looking back through all of my cases and showing that this is not a common finding in the absence of another explanation, that's probably the best observational study that we have currently to say that this is an unusual finding.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. And when you say this is an unusual finding, are you referring to that line of gas that we see --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: -- above the spine of [Baby A] in the radiograph?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: to something that they've had, is it something we can infer something from? And the conclusion of it was that we saw it after traumatic deaths and we think that resuscitation might move some of the gas around the body. That's all we can say from that study. I didn't want to present that study and then draw inferences to the cases we have in front of us today without having made some reference to the types of children that I see on a day-to-day basis.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And the children, they can be from neonates --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: They can.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: -- up to teenage years?

blocks.text: Absolutely. blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So in 500 babies under 1, who, if you take out all of those who were born and never breathed, for example, quite a lot of foetuses and stillbirths, we can find 46 children who had been born and subsequently died in the first few months of life and, of those, we found that six had gas in those locations, all of whom had had trauma to the body, head injuries, road traffic accidents, allowing gas to enter the body through fractures, and the sixth child had died of an overwhelming infection in sepsis. So I'm trying to contextualise from my clinical experience how common it is to see gas in this exact location on a post-mortem radiograph in a child without any history. And the conclusion I've drawn is it's unusual.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There was no formal support, but within the unit we were very supportive of each other, but there was no formal support.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: That's what I wanted just to ask you before I finish.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As between the nurses, you would try to support one another, wouldn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, we would.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: And so if you saw one another, you'd give one another support?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, we would.
blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: next day, I would go to them personally and ask if they were okay. blocks.speaker: BENNION

blocks.text: All right. To a large extent did the nurses have to really just get on with it themselves and deal with it as best they could?

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. You'd staff to a required level and then if you had a few admissions you needed more on a shift than expected then --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. The jury has heard a little bit about the various levels of neonatal unit. There are three levels. And at the time that we're interested in, Chester was a level 2?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: It was, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And I don't think this is controversial, that meant that generally, Chester could accept babies at 27 weeks gestation and above?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But obviously, things didn't always work out as planned, but that was the general rule?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No. If a baby -- if a mum came in and needed to deliver before she could be moved with the baby still in utero, and it was before that time, then the baby would be moved --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- after.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Shift times typically were 7.30 until 8 on days?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And 7.30 until 8 on nights?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Obviously the other end of the clock. But that's generally what it was and there would be an overlap between the two shifts, both at the beginning and at the end?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We've heard a little bit about the handover process.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There'd be a huddle with the new shift, is that right, to discuss general matters?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. We'd get a handover sheet that had the baby's name, basic details, gestation, born at, days old, who was looking at it for that shift, and a summary of how the baby was at that point in time. Then at the bottom there might be points of information that we needed to know, new policies to go and look at or -- you know, safety briefs, we used to call them.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So that was as a team. Then we understand that individual nurses would go to their allocated baby and would have a more, if I can put it this way, detailed handover from the preceding designated nurse?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, and the team leaders would have a more detailed one-to-one about all the babies, so the team leader would, I think -- the team leaders were what they call them where I am now, shift leader, whatever --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay, all right. Did you ever work as a team leader on the shifts at Chester?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We've heard about the different types of nursing levels, there would be level 4s, who I think would be nursery nurses?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Level 5s, who would either have specialty or not, and then level 6s like yourself. All right. Who would allocate babies for each shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Typically it would be the team leader on the shift that was going off, so they'd look at who was coming on, what the babies were requiring, and allocate appropriate --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it wouldn't be the shift leader coming on, it would be the preceding leader knowing who's going to come on and allocating resources accordingly?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. So when you came in, you (inaudible: coughing).
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Again, I don't think we need to go through this in any more detail, but there were effectively four nurseries: nursery 1, which was of the intensive care room; nursery 2, which was the high dependency room; and 3 and 4 which we have heard described as growing rooms.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Would that be fair?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, special care, yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. Was there a distinction between day shifts and night shifts as far as busyness was concerned?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Day shifts tend to be busier in some ways because there's more staff around, so routine investigations, routine procedures, ward rounds, there's more visitors.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In terms of what the babies needed, then that could be the same, but the non-urgent stuff, non-urgent things, examinations could be -- they'd tend to do those in the day --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- so they could be quieter in that sense.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. So do we take it then if the days were busier for all those reasons, the nights were quieter?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, but not necessarily in terms of admissions and, you know, if a baby needed immediate attention.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As many parents around on a night shift as there would be on a day shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No, it was open for visiting for parents, so some of them would stay quite late into the evening, if babies had been on the unit for a while and the dads had had to go back to work, they might come in after work and then go -- we even had dads come in before work. But generally, no, there was -- there were few parents and for the large part just the nurses and nursery nurses because the doctors cross-covered, so they may have been over on the paediatric ward or in A&E.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The babies were monitored on the unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Various things monitored and if those features being monitored fell below certain levels we have heard there would be alarms that would activate?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Was there more than one type of alarm?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. The monitors had three different types of alarms.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So for various reasons, you'd have an upper limit and a lower limit, so whichever aspect that was, you'd set limits, so if... If... If that parameter went above, you'd get an alarm that sounded one way. If things started dropping, there was like a preliminary alarm, so if it dropped within a certain amount below the alarm limit, and then if it dropped below another amount you got a more urgent alarm. So there were different tones.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So urgent alarm and more urgent alarm, would that be a fair way to put it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It might sound a daft question, but if an alarm went off, what would a nurse be expected to do?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Go to the baby if possible.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I say "if possible", because you might be doing something else, but look to see what parameter was alarming, how the baby was looking --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- pay attention.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Assess the situation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. And if there was something wrong, what would you expect the nurse to do?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Deal with it --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- appropriately.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: On their own?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: It would depend what was going on, which alarm, why the alarm was going off. So there's not one straight answer to that. It would depend for the reason that --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Would a doctor be immediately called --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Not necessarily, no. It would depend.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So would the nurse try and resolve it first?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: He did look cyanotic as well.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, that was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Blue, dusky.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Cyanotic" was what you said?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. But it was this purply blotchiness with white that I'd not seen before.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Where was that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Over his body.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Can you tell where in particular on his body it was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No, not for certain. My recollection was it was over him, you know, everywhere, maybe more torso -- no, I can't remember clearly. But I just (inaudible: coughing) unusual.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Anything else you can tell us about that discolouration, anything that sticks in your memory?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: It had come on very suddenly -- just how unusual it was.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. So did [Baby A] respond to your efforts at CPR or the medication he was receiving?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: No.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You told us Dr Harkness was there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Was anybody else summoned?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, other doctors came in. I... I didn't recall from memory, but I knew other doctors had come in. I do know who it was, but -- I knew there were doctors there, I do remember Ravi Jayaram, Dr Jayaram, coming in. I can remember where he was standing.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Was that a request for help, was it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you know who made that request?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I don't know who put the call out, the emergency call out, because Dr Harkness was in the room, so when [Baby A] first didn't respond to Lucy and she asked for help, in fact the registrar was right there, so actually I don't think the call went out as quickly as it -- not that there was a delay because he was already there, so I think the call went out when it became evident that Dr Harkness needed more people, more doctors there...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And how would that call for help go out?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: From the telephone. You dial --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is there a system?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes, there was a specific number that you dialled that went to a specific phone in switch --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: -- so that they would all answer it quickly and then you gave -- it was just "neonatal emergency" and the room.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And then that's a spoken -- rather than it just being a bleep, it's actually spoken out loud.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You were telling us, were you, who then came?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Dr Jayaram, who was the consultant on that night, and I believe Rachel Lambie came well and that Dr Wood was there.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We'll just have a quick look at 197, please, on the sequence of events. That suggests that Dr Jayaram arrived at 8.30.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I -- yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we can work out that's 10 minutes -- you swiped in at 20 past, he swipes in at --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we're talking about 10 minutes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Which is a reasonable response because we had a registrar there, so we were treating, and, you know, it will have taken -- I don't know where Dr Jayaram was at the time he got the call, so...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. Because of what was happening with [Baby A], was a decision made about his parents?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: At the same time that the emergency call went out, I think somebody went to get his parents from -- to come to the unit.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Do you know where they were?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I can't honestly remember if at that point mum was still on delivery suite or if she'd gone up to the post-natal ward. I know it was one or the other.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Once Dr Jayaram had arrived, can you tell us what went on once he'd arrived?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So we continued with the full resuscitation and gave resuscitation medications as well. I know Dr Jayaram spoke to the parents, he... From what I recall, he was standing on my right, the parents were to the right side of the incubator as well, and he was overseeing the resuscitation. And we gave several rounds of adrenaline and each time you give it, you pause and someone listens to see if we've got a heart rate and we didn't ever hear -- well, we did hear one, but not for long and not very fast.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Apart from that, I think we've heard a little bit about that, but apart from that did [Baby A] respond to the treatment that you were giving him?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Not at all.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And did there come a point when Dr Jayaram spoke to the parents?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes. I didn't hear the exact conversation, but he -- I know he was speaking to the parents, so...
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Tell us about the parents at this stage.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So mum and dad, [Mother of Babies A & B] and [Father of Babies A & B], were there and grandma, grandma was with them as well. And I know that towards the end of the resuscitation, after Dr Jayaram had spoken to them, mum was crying and just saying, "Please don't let my boy die".
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did there come a point where treatment was stopped?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: There did, yes. Sadly, in a resuscitation, if a baby's not responding after a certain length of time, despite everything, then you have to stop.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. So what then followed at that point when resuscitation had been stopped?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: So a lot of people would leave the room. There was quite a large number of people in the room at that point in the resuscitation. You've got somebody documenting what's happening, you've got somebody prescribing drugs, you've got people drawing up drugs. You know, there's a lot of people in the room. So everyone that could would leave.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: And then usually, the nurse looking after the baby, the designated nurse, and maybe one other, possibly the consultant, would stay a little longer and we'd disconnect the lines and tubes that we could and pass the babies to the parents to --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You can't disconnect all lines then, is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: We didn't remove lines. We left lines in because it -it was very sudden and very unexpected. So at that time, the decision was made to leave lines in because we didn't know whether the coroner would require a post-mortem or not. So we disconnect lines but we actually left -- you know, we disconnect them and cap them off as close to the babies --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But they're left in situ?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. You told us that everyone who can leave leaves in the aftermath. Were you one of those who had to stay or did you leave?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I can't actually remember that. I know -- I remember being outside the room, but I can't remember how quickly after that I left or whether I stayed to support Lucy for a little while.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did you have a conversation with Lucy afterwards?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did you discuss any steps that might be taken in the immediate aftermath?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I think Lucy -- well, I know Lucy said to me that, you know, the fluids had only just started, we need to keep the bag.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Do you know whether that was actually done?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I don't.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We've heard that in the aftermath of the baby's death, there is a memory box prepared. Did you play any part in that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I don't actually recall. My memories of the actual resuscitation have always been very clear, even before my first interview, but not --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: I may have done, I may not have done.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. You continued for the rest of the night shift thereafter?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: NURSE A: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, I'm about to move on to the following night. I wonder whether that might be a suitable point.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it will take some time, will it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I can do some of it, but I just wondered whether -we had an early resumption. I can carry on if my Lord wishes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I think that'll do for this afternoon.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm afraid it's not going to be possible to complete your evidence this afternoon.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: NURSE A: I was expecting that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You'd probably been told that. An appropriate moment has to be chosen because the questions are now going to turn to [Baby B], so it's a sensible place to break off. Can you come back to continue on Monday morning, please --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: NURSE A: I can.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: -- at 10.30? In the meantime, obviously don't talk to anyone about your evidence, this case or anything to do with it.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: NURSE A: I won't.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Just stay there for the moment, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: All right, members of the jury, 10.30 on Monday morning, please. Thank you very much. And remember your obligations, similarly: no conversations with anyone, no research.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
Mr Astbury, is there someone to look after the witness?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, there is, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: As soon as I've risen, the court should be cleared and that person should come and assist the witness. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The court adjourned until 10.30 am on Monday, 24 October 2022)
